name: Concurrency & Parallelism
description: Threads, locks, races, memory ordering, async models and the deadlocks that eat production systems.

modules.name: Models & Primitives
modules.description: What concurrency is, how it differs from parallelism, and the tools for coordinating work.

cards.answer: Concurrency is dealing with many things at once (structure); parallelism is doing many things at once (execution).

left.title: Concurrency
points: A way of structuring a program
Possible on a single core via interleaving

cards.explanation: Rob Pike's framing: concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once, parallelism is about doing lots of things at once. A concurrent design *enables* parallelism but does not require it — Node.js is concurrent and single-threaded.

resources.title: Rob Pike — Concurrency is not parallelism

cards.answer: Processes have isolated address spaces; threads share one address space within a process.

left.title: Process
points: Crash does not take down siblings
Expensive to create; IPC needed to communicate
True parallelism even with a GIL

right.title: Thread
points: Cheap to create; own stack and registers
Communication by shared memory — needs locks
One bad thread can corrupt the whole process

cards.explanation: The trade is isolation against communication cost. Chrome uses processes per site for security; databases use threads for shared buffer pools. Green threads (goroutines, virtual threads) give thread-like ergonomics at a fraction of the cost.

cards.prompt: Why is this counter wrong under concurrency?
cards.answer: `counter += 1` is read, add, write — three steps. Two threads can read the same value and both write back the same increment, losing updates. Use a lock or an atomic type.
cards.explanation: A data race is unsynchronised access to shared mutable state where at least one access is a write. The classic fixes: a mutex, an atomic operation, a compare-and-swap loop, or removing the sharing entirely (per-thread accumulators merged at the end).

cards.answer: A mutex is binary ownership — the locker must unlock. A semaphore is a counter permitting N holders, and any thread may signal it.

left.title: Mutex
points: Mutual exclusion for a critical section

cards.explanation: Use a mutex to protect data, a semaphore to limit resource concurrency (connection pools, rate limits) or to signal between threads. Condition variables handle 'wait until a predicate holds' — always re-check the predicate in a loop, because of spurious wakeups.

cards.prompt: What four conditions must hold simultaneously for deadlock, and how do you prevent it in practice?
cards.answer: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one — in practice you impose a global lock ordering to kill circular wait, or use timeouts and try-lock to break hold-and-wait.
cards.explanation: Lock ordering is the cheapest discipline: assign every lock a rank and always acquire in ascending order. Other practical rules: never call unknown code while holding a lock, keep critical sections tiny, and prefer lock-free queues or message passing where possible.

modules.name: Memory Models & Patterns
modules.description: Visibility, atomics, lock-free thinking and the async concurrency models.

cards.prompt: Why can one thread's write be invisible to another even after it completes?
cards.answer: Compilers and CPUs reorder and buffer memory operations. Without a synchronisation edge — a lock, an atomic with the right ordering, a volatile/fence — there is no guarantee another thread ever observes the write, or observes writes in program order.
cards.explanation: Memory models define these guarantees as happens-before relationships, not as caches. Sequential consistency is the intuitive model; acquire/release is the cheap one that still orders everything before a release against everything after the matching acquire.

resources.title: Preshing — Memory ordering at compile time and runtime

cards.prompt: What is compare-and-swap, and what is the ABA problem?
cards.answer: CAS atomically sets a location to a new value only if it currently equals an expected value, reporting success. ABA is when a value changes A→B→A between your read and your CAS, so the CAS succeeds even though the state was mutated meanwhile.
cards.explanation: CAS underpins lock-free stacks, queues and atomic counters, usually in a retry loop. ABA is defused with versioned pointers (a counter packed alongside), hazard pointers, or epoch-based reclamation — which is the hard part of lock-free data structures.

cards.prompt: Two threads increment two different counters and the program gets *slower* with more threads. Why?
cards.answer: False sharing: the counters sit in the same 64-byte cache line, so each write invalidates the other core's copy and the line ping-pongs between caches. Pad or align each counter to its own cache line.
cards.explanation: Cache coherence works per line, not per variable. Fixes: `alignas(64)` / `@Contended`, per-thread accumulators combined at the end, or striped counters (LongAdder). It is invisible in the code and obvious in a profiler's cache-miss counters.

cards.answer: Thread-per-request writes naturally and blocks freely but costs memory per connection; an event loop handles huge connection counts on few threads but forbids blocking.

left.title: Thread per request
points: Virtual threads remove most of the cost

right.title: Event loop
points: Callback/async colouring spreads through the code
Excellent for I/O-bound proxies and gateways

cards.explanation: The models converge: Go and Java 21 give you blocking-style code on cheap green threads with an event loop underneath. The rule that never changes is that CPU-bound work must leave the I/O thread.

cards.prompt: A payment request times out and the client retries. How do you avoid charging twice?
cards.answer: Make the operation idempotent: the client sends an idempotency key, the server records the key with the result in the same transaction, and a repeat of that key returns the stored result rather than re-executing.
cards.explanation: At-least-once delivery is what networks actually give you, so exactly-once *processing* is built from idempotency plus deduplication. The key must be persisted atomically with the effect — otherwise a crash between them reopens the window.
